Q1.text: The goal is to build a foundation model for image segmentation that can be prompted, similar to how language models are prompted, and that generalizes zero-shot to new data distributions and tasks.
The paper frames the problem as three entangled questions: what task enables zero-shot generalization, what model architecture fits it, and what data can power it.

Q2.text: Foundation models pre-trained on web-scale data have driven strong zero-shot and few-shot generalization in NLP and, to a lesser extent, vision-language tasks.
Segmentation covers a wide range of computer vision problems for which abundant training data does not exist, unlike text-image pairs available on the web.

Q3.text: There is no web-scale data source for segmentation masks, unlike the web-scale text and image-text corpora that power other foundation models.
Prior multi-task segmentation systems perform a fixed set of tasks where training and test tasks are the same, unlike a model that can perform new tasks at inference time via prompting.

Q4.text: The authors introduce a promptable segmentation task, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with an image encoder, prompt encoder, and mask decoder, and a data engine used to collect the SA-1B dataset.
SAM predicts multiple (by default 3) candidate masks per prompt along with a predicted IoU confidence score to handle prompt ambiguity.
The data engine has three stages: assisted-manual annotation, semi-automatic annotation, and fully automatic mask generation, which together collected 1.1B masks on 11M images.
Given a precomputed image embedding, the prompt encoder and mask decoder predict a mask in about 50 milliseconds in a web browser.

Q5.text: The model separates a heavyweight image encoder (run once per image) from a lightweight prompt encoder and mask decoder so the image embedding cost can be amortized across many different prompts.
SAM predicts multiple masks per ambiguous prompt because a single averaged mask would be invalid when a prompt (e.g., a point on a shirt) could refer to more than one object.
The authors chose an MAE-pretrained Vision Transformer image encoder, motivated by scalability and access to strong pretraining.

Q6.text: The paper reports five zero-shot transfer experiments: single-point valid mask evaluation on 23 datasets, edge detection on BSDS500, object proposal generation on LVIS, instance segmentation on COCO/LVIS, and a text-to-mask proof-of-concept.
The paper also runs a Responsible AI fairness analysis measuring SAM's segmentation performance across perceived gender presentation, age group, and skin tone.
Ablation experiments vary the data-engine training stage, the amount of SA-1B training data (0.1M/1M/11M images), and the image encoder size (ViT-B/L/H).

Q7.text: SAM produces higher mIoU than the RITM baseline on 16 of 23 zero-shot single-point segmentation datasets, by as much as about 47 IoU.
Using an oracle that picks the best of SAM's 3 predicted masks, SAM outperforms RITM on all 23 datasets.
On BSDS500 zero-shot edge detection, SAM scores ODS .768, OIS .786, AP .794, R50 .928, compared to the learned HED baseline's ODS .788, OIS .808, AP .840, R50 .923.
On LVIS instance segmentation, SAM achieves AP 44.7 versus the fully-supervised ViTDet-H's AP 46.6; on COCO, SAM achieves AP 46.5 versus ViTDet-H's AP 51.0.
In a human 1-10 mask-quality rating study, SAM (mean 8.1) rated higher than ViTDet-H (mean 7.9) on LVIS despite SAM's lower AP.
On a 500-image sample of automatically generated masks, 94% of pairs (automatic vs. professionally corrected) exceeded 90% IoU agreement, and 97% exceeded 75% IoU.

Q8.text: The results establish that SAM's zero-shot single-point segmentation is competitive with, and often better than, a strong prior interactive segmentation baseline (RITM) across a diverse 23-dataset suite.
The results establish that automatically generated SA-1B masks are of high quality, closely matching professional corrections at a level exceeding reported prior inter-annotator consistency.

The results establish that SAM can be composed with an existing object detector (ViTDet) to perform zero-shot instance segmentation, trailing but reasonably close to the fully-supervised specialist model in AP.

The fairness analysis establishes that within most gender, age, and skin-tone groupings, SAM's person-segmentation performance confidence intervals overlap, with older vs. middle age being the stated exception.

Q9.text: The results do not establish a quantitative measure of the text-to-mask capability; it is presented only as a qualitative proof-of-concept that the authors call exploratory and not entirely robust.
The results do not establish that SAM matches dedicated interactive segmentation methods when many points are provided; the authors state such methods are expected to outperform SAM in that regime.
The fairness-by-skin-tone results rely on a proprietary dataset not released with the paper, so that part of the analysis cannot be independently reproduced from released artifacts.
The paper does not claim SAM's overall pipeline is real-time when using the heavy image encoder; only the prompt encoder and mask decoder stage is near-real-time given a precomputed embedding.

Q10.text: The authors state their principal contributions are a new task (promptable segmentation), a new model (SAM), and a new dataset (SA-1B) intended to bring image segmentation into the era of foundation models.

Q11.text: SAM can miss fine structures, occasionally hallucinates small disconnected components, and does not produce boundaries as crisp as more computationally intensive zoom-in methods.
Dedicated interactive segmentation methods are expected to outperform SAM when many points are provided, since SAM is designed for generality rather than high-IoU interactive segmentation.
SAM's overall performance is not real-time when using a heavy image encoder, even though the prompt encoder and mask decoder run in about 50ms.
It is unclear how to design simple prompts that implement semantic and panoptic segmentation with SAM.
SA-1B, as released, includes only the automatically generated masks from the final data-engine stage, not the manual or semi-automatic stage masks.

Q12.text: Segment Anything introduces a promptable segmentation task, the SAM model, and the SA-1B dataset of over 1.1 billion masks on 11 million images, aiming to make segmentation a foundation-model-style capability.

SAM's zero-shot performance is often competitive with or superior to prior fully supervised results across several segmentation-related tasks, though it generally trails specialist fully-supervised models on strict AP metrics.
The model, given a precomputed image embedding, produces a mask from a prompt in about 50 milliseconds, enabling real-time interactive use in a browser.
